subject: using measEq.syntax() with the Industrialization and Political Democracy dataset

messages.author: 3e4a285e4828dcad
messages.subject: using measEq.syntax() with the Industrialization and Political Democracy dataset
parts:
Hi,
I am using the Political Democracy dataset with the measEq.syntax() function as a pedagogical exercise. I take the model syntax for this dataset from Rosseel 2019. 

I find that I cannot generate model syntax with measEq.syntax() that produces a reasonable fit. With the complete syntax:

mod.cat.complete <- '

# latent variable definitions
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
 
# regressions
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
 
# residual (co)variances
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y4 + y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  y6 ~~ y8
'
...the fit of course looks reasonable, but if I remove the residual (co)variances syntax I have this:

mod.cat.partial <- '

# latent variable definitions
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
 
# regressions
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
'
...as the configural model in measEq.syntax():

syntax.partial <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat.partial,
                               data = PoliticalDemocracy,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "marker",
                               ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016")

Then the fit statistics generated with:

syntax.partial.fit <- sem(as.character(syntax.partial),
                          data = PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(syntax.partial.fit)

...are considerably worse compared to what I see with:

mod.complete.fit <- sem(mod.cat.complete,
                           data = PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(mod.complete.fit)

I am wondering what I need to add to the syntax in mod.cat.partial in order to achieve a reasonable fit (short of providing the complete syntax)?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: using measEq.syntax() with the Industrialization and Political Democracy dataset
parts:
First, this has nothing to do with measEq.syntax().  When you fix 6 parameters to zero (whose estimates are substantially nonzero) rather than estimating them, your model fit of course gets worse.  Just run the help-page example and then again omit the residual covariances to verify:

example(sem)
mod2 <- '# latent variable definitions

ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
 
# regressions
  dem60 ~ ind60

dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60 '
fit0 <- sem(mod2, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(semTools::compareFit(fit, fit0))

Second, measEq.syntax() is for testing invariance in CFAs, so don't include regressions among common factors (the predictors might be misinterpreted as higher-order factors; read the help page).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

parts:
Thank you for the quick response. I did not intend to fix 6 parameters to zero. What input argument have I inadvertently used in the measEq.syntax function to fix these parameters?
According to the measEq.syntax help page, ID.fac = "UL" avoids 'complications with differentiating lower-order vs higher-order...factors'. I do not understand how this might avoid dem60 and dem65 being misinterpreted. I would have thought that because the variable names are identical in the 'latent variable definitions' and 'regressions' section of the model specification, dem60 and dem65 could be readily recognised as lower-order factors.

Thanks again.

Again, it has nothing to do with measEq.syntax().  Review your syntax in your first post.
According to the measEq.syntax help page, ID.fac = "UL" avoids 'complications with differentiating lower-order vs higher-order...factors'.
You are not fitting a higher-order factor model, so that statement from the help page had nothing to do with what you are doing.
